los.text: Describe the subdivisions of the thorax
los.html:
Thoracic cavityTwo pulmonary cavities (pleura and lungs) either side of the central mediastinum.
Superior mediastinum
  • Above the plane of the sternal angle (T4/5): thymus remnant
  • Arch of aorta and its branches
  • Brachiocephalic veins and upper SVC
  • Trachea
  • Oesophagus
  • Vagus and phrenic nerves
  • Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Thoracic duct.
Inferior mediastinumBelow that plane, split by the pericardium into:
AnteriorBehind the sternum: thymus remnants, fat, lymph nodes.
MiddleHeart and pericardium, roots of the great vessels, phrenic nerves.
PosteriorDescending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos/hemiazygos veins, vagus nerves (sympathetic trunks lie alongside).
Sternal angle (T4/5, 2nd costal cartilage): carina, start and end of the aortic arch, azygos joins the SVC.

los.text: List the structures of the thoracic wall including the thoracic spine, ribs, and sternum, and describe the articulations of these bones
los.html:
Bones12 thoracic vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs with costal cartilages, sternum (manubrium, body, xiphoid).
RibsTrue 1–7 (own cartilage to sternum); false 8–10 (cartilage joins the one above); floating 11–12.
Typical rib (3–9)Head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, shaft with the costal groove on its inferior border.
Atypical1st (short, flat, broad; scalene tubercle; grooves for subclavian vein in front and artery behind); 2nd; 10th–12th (single head facets).
JointType
Costovertebral (rib head with two vertebral bodies and disc)Synovial plane
Costotransverse (tubercle with transverse process, ribs 1–10)Synovial plane
1st sternocostalPrimary cartilaginous (synchondrosis)
2nd–7th sternocostalSynovial plane
Costochondral (rib to its cartilage)Primary cartilaginous
Interchondral (cartilages 6–9/10)Synovial plane
Manubriosternal (sternal angle)Secondary cartilaginous (symphysis)
XiphisternalPrimary cartilaginous (often ossifies)

los.text: Describe how the boundaries of the thoracic inlet and outlet are formed by the vertebrae, ribs, costal cartilages and sternum
los.html:
Superior thoracic aperture (inlet)
  • Body of T1 behind, first ribs and cartilages at the sides, jugular notch of the manubrium in front
  • Slopes down anteriorly.
Passes through the inletTrachea, oesophagus, great vessels, vagus and phrenic nerves, sympathetic trunks, thoracic duct; lung apices (cervical pleura) bulge up through it.
Inferior thoracic aperture (outlet)T12 behind, ribs 11–12, costal margin (cartilages 7–10) and xiphisternal joint; closed by the diaphragm.
Diaphragm openingsIVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12 ("I 8 10 Eggs At 12").
Clinical "thoracic outlet syndrome"(really the inlet)a cervical rib or scalene band compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus or the subclavian artery.

los.text: Identify the thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum and the joint types between them
los.html:
Thoracic vertebra
  • Heart-shaped body
  • Costal demifacets on the body for rib heads
  • Transverse costal facets (T1–10) for rib tubercles
  • Long spinous process sloping down
  • Small round vertebral foramen
  • Facet joints in the coronal plane (rotation, little flexion).
SternumManubrium (jugular notch, clavicular notches, 1st cartilage); body (2nd cartilage at the sternal angle, then 3rd–7th); xiphoid.
Rib count from the frontFind the sternal angle → 2nd costal cartilage → count down the intercostal spaces.
Joint typesSee LO 2 (costovertebral and costotransverse synovial; 1st sternocostal and costochondral primary cartilaginous; manubriosternal secondary cartilaginous).

los.text: Label a diagram of the basic structure of the airway, summarising the anatomy of the bronchial tree and bronchopulmonary segments, and explain their functional significance in relation to inhalation injury
los.html:
TracheaC6 (cricoid) → T4/5 (carina); 10–12 cm; 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilages, gap behind closed by trachealis.
Branching(~23 generations)
  • Main bronchi
  • → lobar (3 right, 2 left)
  • → segmental
  • → bronchioles
  • → terminal bronchioles (end of conducting zone)
  • → respiratory bronchioles
  • → alveolar ducts
  • → alveoli (respiratory zone).
Right main bronchusShorter, wider and more vertical → inhaled objects usually go right (right lower lobe; if supine, posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe).
Bronchopulmonary segment
  • Wedge supplied by its own segmental bronchus and pulmonary artery branch (central)
  • Drained by veins in the intersegmental septa
  • Can be removed surgically on its own.
LobeRight segmentsLeft segments
UpperApical, posterior, anteriorApicoposterior, anterior, superior and inferior lingular
MiddleLateral, medial(none)
LowerSuperior, medial/anterior/lateral/posterior basalSuperior, anteromedial, lateral and posterior basal
  • Inhalation injury: hot gas burns mainly the airway above the vocal cords → oedema, stridor, early intubation
    • smoke chemicals injure lower airways
    • carbon monoxide and cyanide poison systemically.

los.text: List the relations of the trachea and be able to identify them
los.html:
RelationNeckThorax
AnteriorThyroid isthmus (rings 2–4), strap muscles, inferior thyroid veinsManubrium, thymus remnant, left brachiocephalic vein, brachiocephalic trunk, arch of aorta
PosteriorOesophagus; recurrent laryngeal nerves in the tracheo-oesophageal groovesOesophagus, vertebral column
RightThyroid lobe, carotid sheathRight vagus, arch of azygos, right pleura and lung
LeftThyroid lobe, carotid sheathArch of aorta, left common carotid and subclavian arteries, left vagus, left recurrent laryngeal nerve

los.text: Identify the features of each lung (and list the differences between left and right lungs)
los.html:
FeatureRight lungLeft lung
Lobes3 (upper, middle, lower)2 (upper with lingula, lower)
FissuresOblique + horizontalOblique only
ShapeShorter and wider (liver pushes diaphragm up)Longer and narrower
Anterior borderStraightCardiac notch
Main bronchusShorter, wider, more verticalLonger, narrower, more horizontal
HilumUpper lobe bronchus above the artery (eparterial)Pulmonary artery highest
Segments108–10
  • Each lung: apex (2–3 cm above the medial clavicle), base on the diaphragm
    • costal, mediastinal and diaphragmatic surfaces
    • anterior, posterior and inferior borders.

los.text: Draw and describe the topographical surface projections of the lungs and parietal pleural reflections of the thoracic wall
los.html:
LineLung edgeParietal pleura
Apex2–3 cm above medial third of clavicleSame
AnteriorRight: down the midline to 6th cartilage; left: to 4th cartilage then out (cardiac notch) to 6thRight to 6th; left to 4th then 6th
Midclavicular line6th rib8th rib
Midaxillary line8th rib10th rib
Paravertebral (posterior)10th rib12th rib
Costodiaphragmatic recess~2 rib spaces of pleura below the lung edge: effusions collect here.
Oblique fissureT2/3 spinous process → along the 5th rib → 6th costal cartilage in front.
Horizontal fissure (right)Along the 4th costal cartilage to meet the oblique fissure at the midaxillary line.

los.text: Identify the lobes and fissures of the lungs on suitable models or prosections and describe their major anatomical relationships to the ribs, heart, aorta and other major vessels of the thorax
los.html:
Lobes from the outside
  • Upper lobes mostly in front and above
  • Lower lobes mostly behind (listen posteriorly)
  • Right middle lobe in front, below the 4th cartilage.
Right mediastinal relationsRight atrium (cardiac impression), SVC, azygos arch, oesophagus, IVC.
Left mediastinal relationsLeft ventricle (deep cardiac impression), arch and descending aorta, left subclavian and common carotid arteries, oesophagus near the base.
Fissure surface linesSee LO 8.

los.text: Locate the impressions made in the left lung by the heart and the aorta
los.html:
Cardiac impressionDeep hollow in front of and below the hilum (left ventricle), with the cardiac notch and lingula on the anterior border.
Aortic grooveArches over the hilum (arch of aorta) and runs down behind it (descending aorta).
Other groovesLeft subclavian artery above the arch; oesophagus near the base.

los.text: Identify the root of the lung and the structures that form it as they enter and leave the lung, and its hilum
los.html:
Hilum
  • The area on the mediastinal surface where structures enter and leave.
  • Root: the bundle of those structures, wrapped in a sleeve of pleura that hangs down as the pulmonary ligament.
ContentsMain bronchus, one pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymphatics and hilar nodes, pulmonary plexus.
Front to backVeins, artery, bronchus.
LowestPulmonary veins (inferior pulmonary vein lowest).
Mnemonic RALSPulmonary artery is anterior to the bronchus on the right, superior on the left.
Relations of the rootPhrenic nerve in front, vagus behind; azygos arches over the right root, aortic arch over the left.

los.text: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the lung and its medical significance (very briefly)
los.html:
Route
  • Superficial (subpleural) and deep (peribronchial) plexuses
  • → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes
  • → tracheobronchial (carinal)
  • → paratracheal
  • → bronchomediastinal trunks
  • → right lymphatic duct / thoracic duct.
CrossoverThe left lower lobe drains partly to right-sided nodes.
Significance
  • Lung cancer spreads along this chain (staging: hilar N1, ipsilateral mediastinal N2, contralateral or supraclavicular N3)
  • Enlarged hilar nodes show on CXR (cancer, TB, sarcoid)
  • Subcarinal nodes widen the carina.

los.text: Describe the nerve supply of lung structures (phrenic and vagus nerves, sympathetic fibres)
los.html:
NerveSupplies
Vagus (parasympathetic, via pulmonary plexus)Bronchoconstriction, ↑ mucus, cough and stretch afferents
Sympathetic (T1–4)Bronchodilation (β2), vasoconstriction
Phrenic (C3–5)Motor to diaphragm; sensory to mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura (pain to the shoulder tip)
Intercostal nervesCostal and peripheral diaphragmatic parietal pleura (sharp localised pain)
  • Visceral pleura and lung tissue: autonomic only, so not painful; pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura.

los.text: Identify the trachea, bronchi, hila, lung fields and diaphragm on a chest radiograph
los.html:
TracheaCentral (slightly right at the aortic knuckle); carina at T4/5.
Hila
  • Left hilum higher than the right (left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus)
  • Made mainly of pulmonary arteries and upper lobe veins.
Lung fieldsDescribed as zones (upper, mid, lower), not lobes; vessels fade towards the periphery.
DiaphragmRight hemidiaphragm higher (liver); gastric bubble under the left; sharp costophrenic angles.
Good inspirationAbout 6 anterior ribs (or 10 posterior) above the diaphragm in the midclavicular line.
